lead: On a rough incline, gravity has two jobs: W sin θ pulls the block down the slope, and W cos θ presses it into the slope. The slope pushes back with normal reaction N = W cos θ, so the largest friction available is μN = μW cos θ. A force P parallel to the plane must beat W sin θ but not exceed the friction limit. This decides whether a load on a ramp, a truck on a ghat road, or a block in a lab will stay put.
prereq: You need: free-body diagrams and particle equilibrium from Equilibrium of a particle, and the friction limit from Laws of friction.

sections.h3: Resolve the weight and find the normal reaction

blocks.text: Draw the free body diagram with axes along and perpendicular to the plane. The weight W acts vertically down. Split it into two perpendicular parts: W sin θ down the slope and W cos θ into the slope. Here W is the weight in N, θ is the angle the plane makes with the horizontal, and both parts are in N. The normal reaction N acts perpendicular to the plane, away from it. No motion occurs perpendicular to the plane, so forces balance: N = W cos θ. For W = 100 N and θ = 30°, N = 100 × cos 30° = 86.6 N.

Friction acts along the plane, not along the weight. Its maximum value is μN, so on an incline the limit is μW cos θ, not μW. Let μ be the coefficient of static friction; it has no units. For μ = 0.3, μN = 0.3 × 86.6 = 26.0 N. The normal reaction is smaller than the weight because only the perpendicular component W cos θ of the weight presses on the plane; the rest, W sin θ, acts along the plane. A steep plane has small cos θ, so it offers little normal reaction and little friction.
N = W cos θ,   f_max = μN = μW cos θ
blocks.where: N is the normal reaction in N; W is the weight in N; θ is the plane angle to the horizontal in degrees; μ is the coefficient of static friction, no units; f_max is the limiting friction in N.

sections.h3: Friction direction and the safe range of P

blocks.text: Take P as a force applied parallel to the plane and directed up the slope. For impending motion down the plane, friction points up the plane. Then P + f = W sin θ, so P = W sin θ − f. At the limit f = μW cos θ, this is the smallest force that can hold the block: P_min = W sin θ − μW cos θ.

For impending motion up the plane, friction points down the plane. Then P = W sin θ + f, and the largest force before sliding starts is P_max = W sin θ + μW cos θ. Any P between P_min and P_max keeps the block in equilibrium. If θ ≤ φ, then P_min ≤ 0 and the block stands on its own; the safe range is then 0 ≤ P ≤ P_max, and P_min only gives the down-the-plane force needed to start sliding down. Use P_min = W sin θ − μW cos θ only when θ > φ. With W = 100 N, θ = 30°, μ = 0.3: W sin θ = 50 N, μW cos θ = 26.0 N, so 24.0 N ≤ P ≤ 76.0 N. At P_min friction is up; at P_max friction is down.
P_min = W sin θ − μW cos θ,   P_max = W sin θ + μW cos θ
blocks.where: P_min is the smallest force in N for equilibrium; P_max is the largest force in N for equilibrium; W is the weight in N; θ is the plane angle in degrees; μ is the coefficient of static friction, no units.

blocks.text: The angle of repose is the steepest angle at which the block stays without any P. Set P_min = 0: W sin θ = μW cos θ, so tan θ = μ. Hence the angle of repose is φ = tan⁻¹ μ, where φ is measured from the horizontal. If θ < φ, the block stays with P = 0. If θ = φ, it is just about to slide. If θ > φ, the block slides down unless a force P is applied. Equivalently, the block stays by itself only when θ ≤ φ, that is μ ≥ tan θ. Some syllabi call the whole topic equilibrium on a rough inclined plane.

items: Draw the free body diagram. Show W vertically down, N perpendicular to the plane, friction f along the plane, and P parallel to the plane.
Resolve W. Compute W sin θ along the plane and N = W cos θ perpendicular to the plane.
Compute the friction limit f_max = μN. Never use N = W on an incline.
Decide impending motion. Down the plane means friction acts up the plane. Up the plane means friction acts down the plane.
Write equilibrium along the plane with the correct signs. If θ > φ, quote P_min ≤ P ≤ P_max; if θ ≤ φ, use 0 ≤ P ≤ P_max.
If no P is applied, compare θ with the angle of repose φ = tan⁻¹ μ.

figure.caption: The chain shows the numbers for W = 100 N, θ = 30°, μ = 0.3: N is W cos θ, friction limit is μN, and P must lie between P_min and P_max. Notice friction reverses direction at the two ends of the range.

spec.title: Block on a rough incline
spec.aria: A block on a rough incline with weight 100 N, angle 30 degrees, normal 86.6 N, friction limit 26.0 N, and the force range 24.0 N to 76.0 N.

examples.question: A block of weight 100 N rests on a plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction is μs = 0.3. A force P is applied parallel to the plane. Find the range of P that keeps the block in equilibrium.
steps: Resolve the weight: W sin θ = 100 × sin 30° = 50.0 N down the plane; W cos θ = 100 × cos 30° = 86.6 N into the plane.
Normal reaction: N = W cos θ = 86.6 N.
Limiting friction: f_max = μs N = 0.3 × 86.6 = 25.98 N, about 26.0 N.
Impending motion down the plane: friction acts up. P_min + f_max = W sin θ, so P_min = 50.0 − 26.0 = 24.0 N.
Impending motion up the plane: friction acts down. P_max = W sin θ + f_max = 50.0 + 26.0 = 76.0 N.
The block stays in equilibrium for 24.0 N ≤ P ≤ 76.0 N. Below 24.0 N it slides down; above 76.0 N it slides up.
examples.answer: The required range is 24.0 N ≤ P ≤ 76.0 N.
examples.check:
import math
W = 100.0
theta = math.radians(30.0)
mu = 0.3
N = W * math.cos(theta)
f = mu * N
P_min = W * math.sin(theta) - f
P_max = W * math.sin(theta) + f
print(round(P_min, 1))
print(round(P_max, 1))

traps: Using N = W instead of N = W cos θ. On an incline the normal reaction is reduced by cos θ, so friction is also reduced.
Putting friction in the wrong direction. Friction always opposes impending motion: up the plane when the block is about to slide down, down the plane when it is about to slide up.
Writing P_min = W sin θ − μW instead of W sin θ − μW cos θ. The friction limit uses the normal reaction, not the full weight.
Forgetting that μ has no units. Friction force, normal reaction and P are all in N.
Treating P_min and P_max as exact motion values. They are the limits of equilibrium; any value between them is also safe.

quiz.q: State the normal reaction on a block of weight W resting on a rough plane inclined at θ to the horizontal.
quiz.a: N = W cos θ, acting perpendicular to the plane.

quiz.q: Why is the friction limit on an incline μW cos θ and not μW?
quiz.a: Friction is limited by μN. On an incline the normal reaction is N = W cos θ, so the limit is μW cos θ. The component W cos θ is smaller than W.

quiz.q: A 100 N block lies on a 45° incline with μ = 0.2. Find N and the range of P parallel to the plane.
At θ equal to the angle of repose and P = 0, what is about to happen? What if θ is slightly larger?
quiz.a: At θ = φ, the block is just about to slide down under its own weight, with friction at its limiting value up the plane. If θ is slightly larger, friction cannot hold it and the block slides down without any P.

quiz.q: For impending motion up the plane, which way does friction act and why?
quiz.a: Friction acts down the plane. The block is about to move up, so friction opposes that impending motion.

quiz.q: A block stays on a 25° incline with no applied force. Find the smallest coefficient of static friction needed.
quiz.a: Use tan θ = μ at the angle of repose. μ = tan 25° = 0.47.

quiz.q: Why do the formulas P_min = W sin θ − μW cos θ and P_max = W sin θ + μW cos θ not apply when P is vertical?
quiz.a: The formulas assume P is parallel to the plane. A vertical P changes both the along-plane component and the normal reaction, so N is no longer W cos θ. Resolve P into components and redo equilibrium.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same equilibrium check appears in ramp design, retaining walls, conveyor inclines and vehicle braking on ghat roads. In geotechnical work the angle of repose describes a heap of sand or grain, while the friction angle appears in slope-stability charts. Search for angle of repose, slope stability and rough inclined plane friction to go further. Modern contact models replace μN by a state-dependent friction law, but the static limit is still the first check.
